Introduction

Don’t overthink it.

A lot of times, the best setups are simple. After all, the value of a stock at 4 PM is simply the price others are willing to trade with each other at. If your thesis is hard for others to understand it’s unlikely the market will see the same value you do.

I’m mixing things up for this week’s piece. Some of the best trades I’ve made this year weren’t predicated on a long winded thesis of “secret situation the market doesn’t understand”, but rather, “the stock just looks cheap”. Whether it was Heritage Insurance at four times earnings, or Brighthouse Financial at a 60-40% chance of being bought, or even perennial value trap OSB bumbling around at 5x earnings with a big buyback, the setups were simple.

This brings me to the land where cheap is, in fact, the norm: Chinese ADRs.

Despite the incredible run of Baidu and Alibaba, many of their smaller peers have entirely missed the recent rally. A few at 3-4x earnings with sizeable capital return programs are increasingly catching my eye, especially given their liquid options chains.

One of the largest risks when investing in Chinese ADRs is “zeroed” risk, that you wake up one day and discover your entire investment is gone, hence why the entire group tends to trade at a rock-bottom valuation.

Liquid options chains present an opportunity: the ability to dabble in these 3x - 4x names with strong capital allocation programs while hedging nearly all of your downside risk.

Many of these trades are still in the formative stages and I put on most yesterday, but I think the combination of rock-bottom valuations, strong capital allocation programs, aligned insider ownership, and options overlays that substantially eliminate downside risk present a few unique setups with 31% upside potential (if things go right) with just 11-12% downside risk. Without further huffing and puffing, let’s get into it.

Trades

1. Chinese Fintech ADR Basket With Options Overlay (60% QFIN, 40% LX)

The Chinese Fintech sector has been ravaged ever since regulatory changes capped interest rates charged to borrowers at 24% (the regulation were released in April and become effective on October 1, 2025, most companies are already complying).

While the entire sector spirals, two names stand out to me: industry leader Qifu Holdings and buy-now pay-later oriented LexinFintech Holdings

Increased regulation may in fact help Qifu and LexinFintech.

Qfin and LexinFintech have for years been fending off unscrupulous competitors who employ aggressive marketing techniques and “bundled loans” (high APY loans tied to unrelated monthly subscriptions as a method to charge additional interest) to lure unsuspecting customers, hence the need for regulation in the first place. The near total elimination of 24%+ APY loans will eat a decent chunk of Qifu’s, and to a lesser extent Lexin’s profits as they still have some exposure to the 24-36% cohort, but it will gradually benefit them on the expense side.

Qifu and Lexin spend 4x as much on Selling and Marketing as they do on General Administrative Expenses, and the elimination of 24%+ loans will simply price out many of their smaller competitors, pushing large amounts of customers towards Qifu and Lexin as the smaller players crumble.

Qifu is an industry leader with a massive chunk of the instant, general purpose, personal loan segment, and LexinFintech specializes in buy-now pay-later financing through its E-commerce platform “Fenqile”, and is extremely popular with younger borrowers.

Both trade at inexpensive valuations. Qifu at 4.3x earnings and 1.26x Tangible Book (14% insider ownership), and LexinFintech at 3.0x earnings and 1.22x Tangible Book (25% insider ownership). Assuming an entire elimination of 24-36% APY loans (Qifu still participates in this category by referring customers to banks for a fee), Qifu is trading closer to 5x earnings, and LexinFintech closer to 3.5x.

As I’ve said before, in Asia return of capital is much more important than return on capital.

What attracts me to both Qifu and LexinFintech relative to their peers, and the market as a whole, is their improving approach to capital allocation given the extremely low valuation they trade at. Both have industry leading buybacks / dividends, and have largely leaned into buybacks over dividends this year, which is exactly what they should do given the under 4x multiple both of them trade at.

LexinFintech - August 7, 2025:

In accordance with our dividend policy, the board of directors has approved a dividend of US$0.194 per ADS, representing 25% of net income for the first half of 2025. As previously announced, we will increase our dividend payout ratio to 30% of net income for the second half of 2025. On top of cash dividend, we’ve announced a US$50 million share repurchase program on July 21, 2025, along with my personal share purchase of up to US$10 million. We’ll continue to explore various means to deliver value to our shareholders.”

The insider ownership relative to executive compensation is excellent, and I’m especially impressed by the clear dividend policy, and the CEO’s pledge to purchase $10 Million with personal funds alongside the $50 Million buyback, which will be conducted over the next 12 months.

Qifu Holdings - August 15, 2025:

On November 19, 2024, the Board approved a share repurchase plan (the “2025 Share Repurchase Plan”) whereby the Company is authorized to repurchase up to US$450 million worth of its ADSs or Class A ordinary shares over the next 12 months starting from January 1, 2025.

As of August 14, 2025, the Company had in aggregate purchased approximately 7.1 million ADSs on the open market for a total amount of approximately US$277 million (inclusive of commissions) at an average price of US$38.9 per ADS pursuant to the 2025 Share Repurchase Plan.

Many have criticized Chinese ADRs as uninvestable due to the sheer amount of rugpulls and frauds that occur, yet I think the antidote to this concern is sizeable share repurchases and dividends.

Qifu raised $50 Million in its 2018 US IPO and a further $36 Million in its Hong Kong secondary, but has paid hundreds of Millions in dividends and repurchased upwards of $1 Billion of its own ADRs on the open market. Similarly, after raising $100 Million in 2017, LexinFintech has spent approximately $50 Million on repurchases and an additional $55 Million in dividends.

If Qifu and LexinFintech are China rugpulls (which is possible), they are either embezzling funds from their bank partners to fund dividends or buybacks (death penalty in China), or simply lying about the share count and faking repurchases since they have returned capital in excess of what they have raised.

I think the more likely explanation is that their excellent capital allocation has gone unnoticed, and that they are simply lumped in with poorly performing Chinese ADRs as a whole.

Investing in China carries high risk, which is why I think a position in Qifu and LexinFintech, combined with an options overlay, can provide an excellent risk-to-reward setup.

Due to the propensity of Chinese ADRs to act insane, the options curve exhibits a significant IV smile; deep out-of-the-money puts and calls are significantly more expensive on an implied volatility basis than at-the-money options.

What this means is, you can give away a little upside on your position (by selling a covered call) at an elevated IV, and use the proceeds to purchase immediate protection via an at-the-money put, at a lower IV. While Chinese ADRs tend to price this left tail “implosion risk in”, by purchasing put protection subsidized via selling calls, you can protect yourself from this threat and structure an attractive setup.

For Qifu, I’ve paired by long position with a February 2026 45 Call / 30 Put Risk Reversal for $1.60. On 100 shares, I’ve sold 1 February 2026 45 Strike Call for $0.84, and purchased 1 February 2026 30 Strike Put for $2.44, for a net cost of $1.60.

This eliminates downside below $30, while capping upside to $45, up until February 2026.

Given the stock is trading at $32.20, the maximum loss even if the stock drops to zero is $2.20 + $1.60 for the risk reversal, so $3.80 a share (11% of my initial outlay). On the other hand, if Qifu bounces back to $45 (where it was trading at just a few weeks ago) the maximum gain is $11.20 a share, or 31% upside relative to the initial investment.

Qifu is a volatile stock. Within the past twelve months, it has routinely moved 15-20 points in both directions.

By paying $1.60 to limit downside below $30, and retaining upside to $45, we are effectively limiting the left-tail risk present in most Chinese ADRs. Even if the name entirely collapses, our loss is minimal (11%), but if it bounces back to $45, we retain significant upside of 31%.

I’ve put on a similar trade in LexinFintech by purchasing a February 2026 7.50 Call / 5.00 Put Risk Reversal for $0.14.

By selling a February 2026 $7.50 Call for $0.56 and buying a February $5.00 Put for $0.70, I am essentially paying 14 cents to limit all downside below $5, while retaining upside to $7.50.

Given the stock is trading at $5.57, the maximum loss if the stock goes to zero is 71 cents (12.74% of the initial investment), and the maximum gain if the stock returns to or exceeds $7.50 is $1.79 (31.3% of the initial investment).

Given LexinFintech experienced a 500% increase to $12 before falling 56% to $6, all within the last 12 months, I think retaining upside to $7.50 by February 2026 leaves an attractive reward (31%), and that limiting downside below $5.00 prudently minimizes risk.

February 2026 is still 5 months away, a lot can happen until then.

Frankly, I think the options on both sides are underpriced and that Qifu, LexinFintech, and the sector as a whole will either snap back 30-40% over the next half year, or fall a further 20% if the impact on growth is larger than anticipated.

Qifu and LexinFintech are trading at extremely attractive valuations as a result of the regulatory headwind, and I think by pairing a long position in these names with significant repurchases and dividends at just 3-4x earnings with an options overlay that retains 31-36% upside with just 11-12% downside risk, an attractive risk-to-reward setup is present.

To summarize, the trades are:

QFIN 60% Weight:

Long 100 QFIN at 32.2 / Sell 1 February 2026 QFIN 45 Call at 0.84 / Buy 1 February 2026 QFIN 30 Put at 2.44

Maximum Risk: $3.80 Maximum Reward: $11.20

LX 40% Weight:

40% Long 100 LX at 5.57 / Sell 1 February 2026 LX 7.50 Call at 0.70 / Buy 1 February 2026 LX 5.00 Put at 0.56

Maximum Risk: $0.71 Maximum Reward: $1.79

Obviously, if you want to do the trade on 500 or 1,000 shares, you would need to purchase 5 or 10 options contracts to hedge your risk.

Given Qifu is the industry leader, I’ve weighed Qifu at 60% in this basket, and LexinFintech at 40%.

3. Sizing

I’ve sized the basket at around 1.5% of NAV, given the trade is in the early stages and I want to leave myself additional room to get aggressive, should the opportunity arise.

Of course, since the downside risk is only 12% (20 bps of NAV) once you put on the options overlay, there’s a lot of room to size this up, but I like to start small and see how things progress.

Frankly, the entirety of the Chinese Fintech sector seems interesting, Jiayfin JFIN would’ve made the basket had the options chain been liquid enough to accommodate a overlay, but when trading Chinese names risk management is paramount which is why I chose to stick to the larger names like Qifu and LexinFintech with liquid options chains and clear capital allocation intentions.

By using an options overlay, we are effectively giving ourselves 3-1 upside, while entirely eliminating the “zeroed” risk that comes so frequently with Chinese ADRs. Given both of these names were trading significantly above the upper bound of the trades just a few weeks ago, I think the risk-to-reward here is attractive enough for a starter position.
